programme: No recognizable module. The concordant set spans mutually unrelated processes with no shared complex or convergent targets: SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling (SMARCC1, which targets its own complex members SMARCB1/SMARCA4), PRC1.1 chromatin regulation (KDM2B), TGFβ-SMAD negative feedback (SKI→SMAD7), chemokine/UPR signaling (CREB3), inflammatory cytokine regulation (ZNF300→SPI1/IL6/CXCL8), glycolysis (ZHX3→HK2), neuronal calcium/ion channel genes (KCNIP3→CACNA1C/CALCA), and a scatter of developmental homeobox/nuclear-receptor TFs (DLX6, EBF2, TFAP2A, SOX8) with no overlapping targets between them.
role_in_a: Not applicable — no coherent programme was found. The one factor with real MS-specific biology, SOX8, acts alone in oligodendrocyte lineage support and remyelination, but nothing among the other ten concordant factors connects to that process, so it cannot anchor a multi-factor programme.
role_in_b: Not applicable — none of the twelve factors has disease-relevant literature support in pancreatic cancer beyond generic Open Targets association scores, so no role for any programme can be stated for disease B.
shared_axis: None identified. No target overlap, complex membership, or documented pathway ties a majority of the concordant factors together, so there is no axis to explain a brain–pancreas connection.
reasoning: Retrieved literature only ever placed two factors in either disease — SOX8 and TET1, both in multiple sclerosis and both in oligodendrocyte/remyelination biology — but TET1 is explicitly marked discordant (its target set did not agree between the two disease-specific networks), disqualifying it from a 'shared' claim, and SOX8 alone is one factor, not a module. The remaining ten concordant factors have no disease-specific literature and their target sets point to at least six unrelated cellular processes with no convergence, so no programme can be named without inventing a mechanism the record does not support (forbidden by rule 5).
support: PMID 39936824 — reviews SOX8 as a developmental TF, general biology not MS-specific but relevant background; PMID 39769160 — SOX8 vs SOX10 activity differences in oligodendroglial cells, places SOX8 in MS-relevant biology; PMID 38097655 — SOX8 required for timely remyelination, places SOX8 in MS but not pancreatic cancer, and connects to no other listed factor; PMID 39770028 and PMID 37286732 — place TET1 in MS oligodendrocyte/demethylation biology, but TET1 is the discordant factor in this pair and so does not support a shared axis.
how_to_falsify: Take the three best chromatin-related candidates (SMARCC1, KDM2B, SKI) and test whether they co-occupy shared regulatory loci in either MS oligodendrocytes/lesion tissue or pancreatic tumor cells using ChIP-seq/CUT&RUN; if their binding sites cluster at common genes (e.g. SWI/SNF-PRC1.1 co-regulated loci) and functional knockdown of any one shifts expression of the others' targets, that would establish a real module and overturn the incoherent verdict. Absent such convergence, the current factor list remains a co-occurrence table, not a mechanism.
caveats: Even the top-ranked concordant factor (SMARCC1) agrees in only 112/286 (39%) of patient-group comparisons, and most sit near 100/286 (~35%) — well under half, so 'concordant' here means a minority plurality, not a robust majority (rule 6). TET1, the only factor with clear literature in either disease besides SOX8, is explicitly discordant and thus excluded from the shared-axis claim. SOX10, the canonical dimerization partner of SOX8 in oligodendrocyte differentiation, is on the tissue-generic exclusion list, which removes the one route by which a genuine oligodendrocyte-programme story could have been built from two SOX factors together. The single-view exclusions (MEF2C, SMAD3, ZIC1, etc.) rule out several plausible-sounding MS-relevant factors as one-cohort artifacts, and none of them can be substituted in regardless. With 286 comparisons drawn from only 3 independent cohort pairs, apparent concordance may also reflect limited cohort diversity rather than a true cross-disease signal.
